title: observe reads an orchestrator that is working as node-stopped once its turn driver has exited
foundBy: session agent operating two eight-member campaigns side by side on one host, reading every member's own CLI session records after both campaigns had ended
details:
**What happened.** For the last forty minutes of a campaign `observe` showed the orchestrator as `node-stopped · m1 · 0 cont, 0 restarts · continue next`. In those forty minutes it accepted a member's reply, wrote and committed the campaign's report, dispatched the final job, merged it and replied to its mission. Nothing was wrong with the campaign. An operator who believed the line would have sent a nudge to an orchestrator that was mid-task, which the playbook rightly calls the most expensive kind of intervention.

**The mechanism.** `protocol.Compute` returns `node-working` only while `Facts.Drivers > 0`, that is, while a turn-driver process is alive for the node's CLI family. A turn driver wraps a turn the host started. The orchestrator here ran on the claude CLI, and it did what its briefing invites: it started a background shell loop that polls `cs-campaign-member observe` until a member is no longer working, said it would wait, and ended its turn. The driver saw the turn end and exited. Minutes later the loop finished, the CLI's own runtime delivered the completion to the session as a new turn, and the session went on working. No driver wraps that turn, because the host did not start it. `Drivers` stays at zero for the rest of the campaign while the session works.

**What follows from it.** Any consumer of "no node is working" is wrong about a live campaign from that moment. A watcher that waits for the campaign to leave `node-working` fires early. The PROTOCOL's statement that *"the orchestrator cannot observe its own death, so the host is the only party that can see it has stopped"* still holds, but the host's view of that one node is now a false positive, and the two cases, an orchestrator that stopped and one that continued itself, print the same line.

**How to reproduce.** Run a campaign whose orchestrator is on the claude CLI. Have its brief tell it to wait for a member by starting a long-running command in the background and ending its turn. After the driver exits, watch the orchestrator's branch: commits keep arriving while `observe` reports `node-stopped · continue next`.

**What would fix it.** Liveness for a node should not rest on the driver alone. The session's own record growing, or the CLI process holding an active turn, is evidence of work that a driver count cannot see. Alternatively the orchestrator's waiting should be something the harness provides and a driver stays alive across, so that an orchestrator never has a reason to end a turn in order to wait.
